blocks.x: Good evening and welcome once again to KBS Radio press conference, which for the next few weeks will be without the familiar voice of Chairman Michael Sumner. Normally in press conference, our personality is connected with the world of politics, government, science, commerce and industry. Tonight is the first time we have had anybody from the world of entertainment. On this occasion, we are delighted to have here in the studio none other than the famous jazz musician Louis Armstrong, affectionately known in households the world over as Satchmo. He'll be questioned by Charles Hayes of East African newspapers, Eric Marsden of the East African standard and Leslie Wink, program organizer of KBS African National Service. Hayes, will you start? Mr. Armstrong, the first thing I understand about you is that nobody calls you Mr. Armstrong. It's always

Satchmo, isn't it? Satchmo, yeah. That's the nickname I picked up in England, you know. In England? Yeah, when I went there in 1932, I met the editor of the Melody Maker, who was Percy Brooks at the time. And at that time, my nickname was Satchel Mouth. See, like the valise, you know what I mean? And now, I don't know, when the train pulled up and Percy Brooks come up, he said, hello, Satchmo, you know. So I said, what'd you say, Daddy? You know, that's what we agreed with. And then I asked my trombone player, who just joined me from Paris, you know. I said, well, why didn't he call me Satchmo? And my name is Satchel Mouth. So the trombone player said, because he thought you had more mouth, you know. Just that easy, I get a nickname. Marsden. Yeah.
Now, I read somewhere, Mr. Armstrong, that Jack Teagarden once described you as just a little guy with a big mouth, but man, can he blow that horn?
That's right.
Now, can you tell us, just how did you learn to blow that horn right now?

Well, I've always been a disciple to Joe Oliver, who was top man when I was a kid. And in the meantime, I used to go around the streets in a little quartet singing, and we'd pass the hat. And I don't know, there was celebration there around New Year's Eve, everybody shoot the big pistols and everything. And my mother kept on trying to hide my stepfather's pistol, but I found it. And I was shooting on Ramport Street, the big street in New Orleans, and the detective hugged me, and I cried like a little baby. But anyhow, they took me to the orphanage, and that's where I learned how to play the trumpet. That's where you got your start. Yeah. First they made me bugle of the institution after six months, you know. And then when I got out, King Oliver taught me how to read music and everything. Wink.
Now, Mr. Armstrong, around about 1930, I remember reading in the paper that you were dead.

Do you remember that? Oh yeah, they always miscalculate there. Ain't nothing to die for, you know, I just told you. If a man takes his stomach, which is the rudimental, it's a big word, that should have been in politics. But same as in Spileto, when I was there, they had in the papers where I was in a coma and things like that, which words I never heard of before I came to Chicago. Because nothing but the rich people went in a coma in New Orleans. We went into trance, maybe. What's the name of the famous?
We're after the essential Satchmo this afternoon. What's your vital statistics? How old?
Well, I'm going to let you guess. I was born in 1900. That's too difficult for me. July 4th.
60 years old, and you can blow that horn that way.
Oh yeah. Smoke? Something in your life. I do all the things you do. Goodness me. You, you, you, you, you.
Now this business in the waif's home, Mr. Armstrong, I believe it was Captain Jones, wasn't it?
Captain Jones. That taught you the bugler.
Was that just one of those little accidents that make history, or would you have been a musician anyway?

That, I don't know, but it happened that way. There's still a way I can, of course, I probably would have been in the music business, probably just singing or something, you know. But I went out there to get the start, because I always followed behind King Oliver in the parades and the funerals, but it never dawned on me that I was going to blow the horn.
Even as a little boy.

A little boy. You followed Mark Johnson. But when they gave me this cornet in the orphanage, I recalled all the things I had been listening to, and I loved the horn, and then by these same people teaching me how to read music, and I went errands, I run errands for Mrs. Oliver. And when he'd lay off, he thought I was good enough to play in his place. That's all right.
And when you got on the riverboats, what was the life like?

Well, it's just the idea that I was on a nicer boat, because I knew the life of riverboats before I got on the steam of Sydney, where Fate Marable used to play the Calypies and things. But before that, we used to unload cotton boats, banana boats. See? I always had the idea of boats, but this was like a dance hall, an excursion boat. And when I got in that band, I kind of feel like I'm a little high up on the horse, you know? You're a composer too, though. Yeah, I wrote a lot of tunes. I wrote Wish I Could Stream Like My Sister Kate, and I play this Stenrichson Barbecue every night. I keep one of my numbers in. But I don't have time to write tunes now. We're traveling so much.
But how do tunes come to you? How do you compose?

Well, all different ways. I wrote a tune called Someday You'll Be Sorry. And I was dreaming of a musical comedy in my sleep, and I couldn't sleep because I had this tune for the theme of the whole play. And I got up in North Dakota one night, freezing, you know? And I got up and got this piece of paper and wrote it down so I could sleep, you know? And my wife raised up and said, are you all right? She thought I was going berserk. So I said, yeah, I'm all right.
But you know how Noel Coward gets into a taxi if he wants to compose? You got any special

gimmick? Well, no, I wouldn't be like him. Because that's just like, all right, can you name somebody a little lesser than Noel? He's the greatest. But you got any special gimmick for composing, or does it just happen? No, you know what? You don't need gimmick. If a tune keeps bothering you and it's on your mind, if you care, write music. Just get somebody to take it down for you. How about that, If We Never Meet Again? Is that yours? Well, with Goylach, I wrote that with a German boy that wrote Swing That Music together. But these are tunes I did myself.
When are you going to play that again? What?

If We Never Meet Again? As soon as I can get the record, because I don't forget to arrange them now myself. I haven't waited in about 30 years. See? And all we do it here is one time and send a repertoire. See?
You know, I've heard your great records from the 20s with Joe Oliver.
Yes, sir.
And I've always been amazed at this improvisation. What's the secret of it? Is it some kind of telepathy?
No, it's a thing I don't know about telepathy, but...
The understanding you have between them.

Oh, I see. Well, that's like I say, if you're serious about your work, it's always a little thing that you can add on yourself and stay to the trend of the music. They call that improvisation or something like that. So I don't have to rehearse the tune for nothing like that. Automatically, it goes in there from the fingers and the way I feel.
It's just natural.

Yeah, that's the way that is. But it's a type of music. And how long do you think that'll go on? How long will the appeal go on? Well, so far, I ain't never felt yet that I didn't want to get up on the stand when it was time. And what about this rock and roll? Well, that's our church music. Church music? Yeah, that's our church music. The old sanctified churches in New Orleans. When I was a kid, the audience would shout and they had a banjo there and everything. So the youngsters, they came in and called it rock and roll, which is not bad. You still got a beat. Still got that beat. But you find that you appeal to the youngsters just the same, don't you? Well, sure. I'm young myself. Yeah. What's your opinion? You can always associate with the youngsters, but just don't try to keep up with them.
What's your opinion of the modern trumpet players who always try to squeeze in the minimum number of notes?

No, well, I don't approve of that because they don't know what they're doing. And they're hitting that notes and praying the Lord to get it. But if I hit a note, I know I'm going to get it because I was taught that way.
Right.

You know? See, that's what I said about this boy. I want to know about modern music. I know what he's aiming at, but just like you said, a whole lot of notes. When you've got one note to hit and they can't do it, they make a thousand notes to get around that one good one because it wasn't trained right.
Mr. Armstrong, I believe you were born on July the 4th. Yes.
It makes you a very much American there.
1900, yeah.
Do you also still think of yourself as an African in many ways?

Yes, I have it in me, man. My great grandparents when I was a kid, I mean, and I met so many Africans in the weather and everything when I was in New Orleans as a child. There have always been Africans all over New Orleans.
Do you ever get any links between New Orleans and Africa? For instance, words like mambo-jumbo. Those are Swahili words, you know?

Yeah. Well, we've used that expression and we had a tune called Mambo-jumbo. Well, those are straight Swahili words. Sure. And we get the same effects. You see that boy beating that drum tonight and he's a Filipina. Mm-hmm. And he's getting the same effect that they get on the drums in Africa. You see what I mean? So it's instilled in everybody from the musical standpoint all over New Orleans for generations.
Is it true that your lips split once when you were playing and you played with blood streaming down your...
Yeah, at the Holborn Empire. Yeah.
How did you manage to carry on?

Well, the show got to go on. That's what killed Boyd Williams. The show business, you know? He'd come out there and they got to push him on the stage. He's so sick. And after he get through, tie it up the house. He'd go back there and fall right out, see? But I didn't do that. It was just one of them things. A cold soul. I should have laid off. I wanted to go on anyway, you know? And it didn't come out right. It just split and I just kept on playing.
Now you switched from the corner to the trumpet a long time ago, didn't you?

Yeah. In 1925. That's because I was playing in a symphony orchestra in 1925 in Chicago for silent pictures. And we used to play Overtures, William Tells, When the Picture Finished. Then after that we played Hot Number. And after that I was there for it, but still in all I had to learn how to play all the classics.
So you're a good sight reader too.
Yeah, we had to do all that, see? And the good old days I'm talking about, you know? Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. as the highest legitimate note on the trumpet, and how far above that can you go?
Well, I can get up to pee. I can whip it.
How do you pick a melody? How do you pick something that you're going to make famous?

Well, we don't look at it from the point that we want to get it to make famous. If you play it good and it sounds good, somebody in the audience is going to like it. And that's the way we do. We like everything we play. See, like we had, if we're never going to meet again, play it, and if the boys would have heard it, we could play it anyhow. See? And it'd be just the same like the record, because all I could do was know the lyrics and everything. But that's things you feel. You don't pick no melody. You don't have to worry about it.
Gentlemen, we've got two more chords to go, so we'll have a quick one from Eric Marsden.

Mr. Armstrong, what about the tribute? You must have had many in your lifetime. I believe the Duke of Windsor, when he was Prince of Wales, once said, I'd rather hear Louis Armstrong play Chinatown than wander into Westminster Abbey and find the lost chord.
There you go.
Have you had any other things like that?
That's a good old number, too. Yeah. Good and fast. I agree with him. Charles Hayes.
Haven't you any plans for issuing an album?
Well, I just made several albums. They are out yet? Yeah, they're not over here. They don't have nothing I made with Ella Fitzgerald.
Yes, that one, but the life story, like the Crosby life story.

Well, I made that, too, for the Decca. That's not out. It's not out here. Not out here. Autobiography, all from the beginning of the tunes I played in England and everywhere, from the old 78s up to the modern-day record. Yeah, it costs $25 in the States. Quick one, Mr. Wayne.
Blue turning gray. Your wife's favorite number, I believe.
Mine, too.
Are we going to hear it here?

Well, we'll play it. Good. We'll play what we can get together on. Because some of them was on that album, Sashmo plays Fats. Yeah. And that's why we can do that, because they was on there. Look forward to that. Yeah.

Well, one thing we've learned from tonight's radio press conference is that it was a mere accident of history that Sashmo learned to play that trumpet when he was taken into an orphanage. Long may he go on playing those golden notes. Your questioners tonight were Charles Hayes of East African Newspapers, Eric Marsden of the East African Standard, and Leslie Wink, program organizer of KBS African National Service. segments.title: Radio press conference opening in Nairobi
segments.summary: Host introduces the KBS press conference and the three questioners.

segments.title: How Armstrong got the nickname Satchmo in England
segments.summary: Armstrong explains Satchel Mouth became Satchmo when Percy Brooks greeted him in England; Teagarden's remark follows.

segments.title: Learning trumpet: the pistol, the orphanage and King Oliver
segments.summary: Armstrong credits Joe Oliver, tells of firing his stepfather's pistol, the orphanage, becoming bugler and learning to read music.

segments.title: Reports of his death and his age
segments.summary: He jokes about being reported dead and 'in a coma', and gives his birth as July 4, 1900.

segments.title: Captain Jones, the waifs' home and following King Oliver
segments.summary: Asked about the waifs' home and whether he'd have been a musician anyway, he recalls following Oliver's parades, running errands for Mrs. Oliver and subbing for him.

segments.title: Riverboat life on the Sidney with Fate Marable
segments.summary: Life on the excursion boat compared with unloading cotton and banana boats; he mentions tunes he has written.

segments.title: How he composes tunes
segments.summary: He describes writing Someday You'll Be Sorry from a dream, says no gimmick is needed, and discusses If We Never Meet Again.

segments.title: Improvisation, rock and roll and young audiences
segments.summary: Asked about improvisation on the 1920s Oliver records, he explains it comes naturally, calls rock and roll church music and speaks of youngsters.

segments.title: Opinion of modern trumpet players
segments.summary: He disapproves of modern players hitting many notes, saying he was trained to hit the right one.

segments.title: Africa and New Orleans: African ties and Swahili words
segments.summary: Asked if he thinks of himself as African, he recalls Africans in New Orleans and Swahili words like mumbo-jumbo and drum effects.

segments.title: Split lip at the Holborn Empire
segments.summary: He recalls playing on with a split lip in London and says the show must go on, citing Bert Williams.

segments.title: Switching from cornet to trumpet; high notes
segments.summary: He switched in 1925 while playing in a Chicago silent-picture orchestra, learning classics, and jokes about high notes.

segments.title: How he chooses melodies
segments.summary: He says he does not pick tunes to make famous; he plays what sounds good and feels right.

segments.title: Tribute from the Prince of Wales
segments.summary: Asked about tributes, he agrees with the Duke of Windsor's remark about Chinatown.

segments.title: Albums, Decca autobiography and a closing request
segments.summary: He discusses albums not on sale locally, the Decca life-story album, and what they will play, including songs from Satchmo Plays Fats.

segments.title: Closing remarks of the press conference
segments.summary: The host sums up and thanks the questioners; the text ends in an ASR loop.
